doc.title: Robert Glasper interviewed by Greg Thomas, Clinton, New York, February 20, 2016

title: Recording Bowie's Letter to Hermione and choosing honest takes
summary: He recorded the Bowie song for Black Radio, and prefers honest takes with band connection over edited solos.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: Oddity,” it’s a very obscure album. But I recorded the song on there called “Letter to Hermione” for “Black Radio” 1 back in 2011. And when I heard it it just reminded me of Bilal. And at that point I didn’t have a song I wanted Bilal to sing yet. And I was just listening to that album, “Space Oddity,” and then that song came on and I was like wow. It was like oh my God. And the way he sings it, if you haven’t heard the original, listen to the original. It’s just David Bowie and guitar and maybe two guitar players. And it’s just so sincere and so honest. You know? And I think that’s what’s missing too, the honesty in the music, which is what also gives people, it makes you different. Because you’re really being honest in what you’re giving. You know what I mean? There’s a lot of songs, even when I’m in the studio I will choose a take even though my piano solo is better on this take, the vibe and the spirit and the honesty of this take is better and I’ll choose that one. You know I don’t like to take solos from here and put them over there. I’m not like that. Because now the bass isn’t — and what I play, the bass player and the drummer are reacting to what I did. So if I move my solo over now it’s sounding like they aren’t with me. The gelling isn’t that spiritual thing, really, the connection isn’t there. But I’ll take a solo that’s not as good because the connection is there, and leave it.
